comments.story: In two incidents, F-16 aviators were rendered unconscious, but saved by software
comments.why: Typical Auto-GCAS recovery footage with HUD altitude readout
comments.text: Assuming we're talking about the typical example ( [VIDEO] ) - in the HUD, altitude is the right-hand vertical tape. (The left one is airspeed.) It looks to bottom out around 4400 feet during the AGCAS recovery.

comments.story: If a pilot ejects, what is the autopilot programmed to do?
comments.why: Example of automation kicking in when plane leaves normal regime
comments.text: Not an expert, but in military planes there are systems which kick in exactly when the plane is outside it's normal regime. Auto-GCAS Saves Unconscious F-16 Pilot: [VIDEO]

comments.author: cbanek
comments.story: Flight QF72: What happens when automation leaves pilots powerless?
comments.why: Example of ground collision avoidance saving an incapacitated pilot
comments.text: That's an excellent point. Even if it's not the people, the stick or manual control inputs are also a point of failure. So if suddenly your stick does something strange, and your flight computer allows it (thinking human knows best) you are in big trouble. The opposite of this is the ground collision avoidance systems, where the humans are one of the weakest parts of the aircraft (due to G-loc). [VIDEO]
